blocks.text: The Act takes place in autumn in a large village. The Scene represents Peter’s roomy hut. Peter is sitting on a wooden bench, mending a horse-collar. Anísya and Akoulína are spinning, and singing a part-song.
We’ll drive ’em in. All in good time.
Ah, but he’s a loafer, that lad﻿ ﻿… no good at all. Won’t stir a finger if he can help it.
You’re so mighty brisk yourself. When you’re not sprawling on the top of the oven you’re squatting on the bench. To goad others to work is all you’re fit for.
If one weren’t to goad you on a bit, one’d have no roof left over one’s head before the year’s out. Oh what people!
You go shoving a dozen jobs on to one’s shoulders, and then do nothing but scold. It’s easy to lie on the oven and give orders.
A colt neighs, the stamping of horses’ feet and the creaking of the gate are heard.
Bragging, that’s what he’s good at. I’d like to sack him, I would indeed.
Where’s Nikíta? Why, standing out there in the street.
What’s he standing there for? He stands there jabbering.
One can’t get any sense out of her! Who’s he jabbering with?
Well, let him go. Just as if I couldn’t find somebody else.
And what about the money he’s had in advance?

Well, of course you’ll be glad if he goes and you’ve not got to feed him. It’s only me as’ll have to work like a horse all the winter. That lass of yours isn’t over fond of work either. And you’ll be lying up on the oven. I know you.
What’s the good of wearing out one’s tongue before one has the hang of the matter?

The yard’s full of cattle. You’ve not sold the cow, and have kept all the sheep for the winter: feeding and watering ’em alone takes all one’s time, and you want to sack the labourer. But I tell you straight, I’m not going to do a man’s work! I’ll go and lie on the top of the oven same as you, and let everything go to pot! You may do what you like.
Puts on a coat and takes a rope.
I’m not going to work for you. You go and work yourself. I’ve had enough of it, so there!
That’ll do. What are you raving about? Like a sheep with the staggers!
You’re a crazy cur, you are! One gets neither work nor pleasure from you. Eating your fill, that’s all you do, you palsied cur, you!
What are you swearing at dad for?
Jumps up and looks round for something to hit her with.
Well, go and marry! What’s that to me?
Yes, go and marry! What do I care?
What are you spitting for? Just see, she won’t even let me stroke her.﻿ ﻿… What’s the matter?
This! That you want to play me false.﻿ ﻿… If you do﻿—why, I don’t want you either. So now you know!

That’ll do, Anísya. Do you think I’ll forget you? Never while I live! I’ll not play you false, that’s flat. I’ve been thinking that supposing they do go and make me marry, I’d still come back to you. If only he don’t make me live at home.
Much need I’ll have of you, once you’re married.
There’s a go now. How is it possible to go against one’s father’s will?

Yes, I daresay, shove it all on your father. You know it’s your own doing. You’ve long been plotting with that slut of yours, Marína. It’s she has put you up to it. She didn’t come here for nothing t’other day.
Marína? What’s she to me? Much I care about her!﻿ ﻿… Plenty of them buzzing around.
Anísya, do you believe in a God or not? I never so much as dreamt of it. I know nothing at all about it. I never even dreamt of it﻿—that’s flat! My old dad has got it all out of his own pate.
If you don’t wish it yourself who can force you? He can’t drive you like an ass.
Well, I reckon it’s not possible to go against one’s parent. But it’s not by my wish.
Don’t you budge, that’s all about it!
There was a fellow wouldn’t budge, and the village elder gave him such a hiding.﻿ ﻿… That’s what it might come to! I’ve no great wish for that sort of thing. They say it touches one up.﻿ ﻿…

Shut up with your nonsense. Nikíta, listen to me: if you marry that Marína I don’t know what I won’t do to myself.﻿ ﻿… I shall lay hands on myself! I have sinned, I have gone against the law, but I can’t go back now. If you go away I’ll﻿ ﻿…

Why should I go? Had I wanted to go﻿—I should have gone long ago. There was Iván Semyónitch t’other day﻿—offered me a place as his coachman.﻿ ﻿… Only fancy what a life that would have been! But I did not go. Because, I reckon, I am good enough for anyone. Now if you did not love me it would be a different matter.
Yes, and that’s what you should remember. My old man will die one of these fine days, I’m thinking; then we could cover our sin, make it all right and lawful, and then you’ll be master here.

Where’s the good of making plans? What do I care? I work as hard as if I were doing it for myself. My master loves me, and his missus loves me. And if the wenches run after me, it’s not my fault, that’s flat.
I only came to get the axe.
I know, sonnie, I know; them sort of axes are mostly to be found where the women are.
Eh, honey! why should you marry? Go on as you are. It’s all the old man. You’d better go, sonnie, we can talk these matters over without you.
What’s it all about then? Do you really wish him to get married?
Where’s the good of my pretending to you, Mother Matryóna? You know all about it. I have sinned. I love your son.
Unties a knot in her handkerchief and brings out paper-packets.
Oh, if only he does not go away.

He won’t go away, birdie. It’s all nonsense. You know my old man. His wits are always woolgathering; yet sometimes he takes a thing into his pate, and it’s as if it were wedged in, you can’t knock it out with a hammer.

Well, you see, my jewel, you yourself know what a fellow with women the lad is﻿—and he’s handsome too, though I say it as shouldn’t. Well, you know, he was living at the railway, and they had an orphan wench there to cook for them. Well, that same wench took to running after him.
Yes, the plague seize her! Whether anything happened or not, anyhow something got to my old man’s ears. Maybe he heard from the neighbours, maybe she’s been and blabbed﻿ ﻿…
Well, she is a bold hussy!

So my old man﻿—the old blockhead﻿—off he goes: “Marry, marry,” he says, “he must marry her and cover the sin,” he says. “We must take the lad home,” he says, “and he shall marry,” he says. Well, I did my best to make him change his mind, but, dear me, no. So, all right, thinks I﻿—I’ll try another dodge. One always has to entice them fools in this way, just pretend to be of their mind, and when it comes to the point one goes and turns it all one’s own way. You know, a woman has time to think seventy-and-seven thoughts while falling off the oven, so how’s such as he to see through it? “Well, yes,” says I, “it would be a good job﻿—only we must consider well beforehand. Why not go and see our son, and talk it over with Peter Ignátitch and hear what he has to say?” So here we are.
Oh dear, oh dear, how will it all end? Supposing his father just orders him to marry her?

Orders, indeed. Chuck his orders to the dogs! Don’t you worry; that affair will never come off. I’ll go to your old man myself, and sift and strain this matter clear﻿—there will be none of it left. I have come here only for the look of the thing. A very likely thing! Here’s my son living in happiness and expecting happiness, and I’ll go and match him with a slut! No fear, I’m not a fool!
And she﻿—this Marína﻿—came dangling after him here! Mother, would you believe, when they said he was going to marry, it was as if a knife had gone right through my heart. I thought he cared for her.

Oh, my jewel! Why, you don’t think him such a fool, that he should go and care for a homeless baggage like that? Nikíta is a sensible fellow, you see. He knows whom to love. So don’t you go and fret, my jewel. We’ll not take him away, and we won’t marry him. No, we’ll let him stay on, if you’ll only oblige us with a little money.
All I know is, that I could not live if Nikíta went away.
Naturally, when one’s young it’s no easy matter! You, a wench in full bloom, to be living with the dregs of a man like that husband of yours.
Mother Matryóna, would you believe it? I’m that sick of him, that sick of this long-nosed cur of mine, I can hardly bear to look at him.

“No sign whatever,” he says. He’s taken a rouble for it. “Can’t sell it for less,” he says. Because it’s no easy matter to get ’em, you know. I paid him, dearie, out of my own money. If she takes them, thinks I, it’s all right; if she don’t, I can let old Michael’s daughter have them.
O-o-oh! But mayn’t some evil come of them? I’m frightened!
What evil, my jewel? If your old man was hale and hearty, ’twould be a different matter, but he’s neither alive nor dead as it is. He’s not for this world. Such things often happen.
O-o-oh, my poor head! I’m afeared, Mother Matryóna, lest some evil come of them. No. That won’t do.
Just as you like. I might even return them to him.
And are they to be used in the same way as the others? Mixed in water?
Better in tea, he says. “You can’t notice anything,” he says, “no smell nor nothing.” He’s a cute old fellow too.
You’ll not forget that rouble? I promised to take it to the old man. He’s had some trouble, too.
Goes to her box and hides the powders.
Well then, how’s it to be, Daddy Akím?

As it’s best, Peter Ignátitch, as it’s best﻿ ﻿… I mean﻿—as it’s best. ’Cos why? I’m afeared of what d’you call ’ems, some tomfoolery, you know. I’d like to, what d’you call it﻿ ﻿… to start, you know, start the lad honest, I mean. But supposing you’d rather, what d’you call it, we might, I mean, what’s name? As it’s best﻿ ﻿…
As to marrying, he might bide a while, Peter Ignátitch. You know our poverty, Peter Ignátitch. What’s he to marry on? We’ve hardly enough to eat ourselves. How can he marry then?﻿ ﻿…
You must consider what will be best.
Where’s the hurry for him to get married? Marriage is not that sort of thing, it’s not like ripe raspberries that drop off if not picked in time.
If he were to get married, ’twould be a good thing in a way.
We’d like to﻿ ﻿… what d’you call it? ’Cos why, you see. I’ve what d’you call it﻿ ﻿… a job. I mean, I’ve found a paying job in town, you know.
And a fine job too﻿—cleaning out cesspools. The other day when he came home, I could do nothing but spew and spew. Faugh!

It’s true, at first it does seem what d’you call it﻿ ﻿… knocks one clean over, you know﻿—the smell, I mean. But one gets used to it, and then it’s nothing, no worse than malt grain, and then it’s, what d’you call it,﻿ ﻿… pays, pays, I mean. And as to the smell being, what d’you call it, it’s not for the likes of us to complain. And one changes one’s clothes. So we’d like to take what’s his name﻿ ﻿… Nikíta I mean, home. Let him manage things at home while I, what d’you call it﻿—earn something in town.
You want to keep your son at home? Yes, that would be well: but how about the money he has had in advance?

That’s it, that’s it! It’s just as you say, Ignátitch, it’s just what d’you call it. ’Cos why? If you go into service, it’s as good as if you had sold yourself, they say. That will be all right. I mean he may stay and serve his time, only he must, what d’you call it, get married. I mean﻿—so: you let him off for a little while, that he may, what d’you call it?

Ah, but it’s not yet settled between ourselves, Peter Ignátitch. I’ll speak to you as I would before God, and you may judge between my old man and me. He goes on harping on that marriage. But just ask﻿—who it is he wants him to marry. If it were a girl of the right sort now﻿—I am not my child’s enemy, but the wench is not honest.
No, that’s wrong! Wrong, I say. ’Cos why? She, that same girl﻿—it’s my son as has offended, offended the girl I mean.
That’s how. She’s what d’you call it, with him, with my son, Nikíta. With Nikíta, what d’you call it, I mean.

You wait a bit, my tongue runs smoother﻿—let me tell it. You know, this lad of ours lived at the railway before he came to you. There was a girl there as kept dangling after him. A girl of no account, you know, her name’s Marína. She used to cook for the men. So now this same girl accuses our son, Nikíta, that he, so to say, deceived her.
Well, there’s nothing good in that.
But she’s no honest girl herself; she runs after the fellows like a common slut.
There you are again, old woman, and it’s not at all what d’you call it, it’s all not what d’you call it, I mean﻿ ﻿…

There now, that’s all the sense one gets from my old owl﻿—“what d’you call it, what d’you call it,” and he doesn’t know himself what he means. Peter Ignátitch, don’t listen to me, but go yourself and ask anyone you like about the girl, everybody will say the same. She’s just a homeless good-for-nothing.
You know, Daddy Akím, if that’s how things are, there’s no reason for him to marry her. A daughter-in-law’s not like a shoe, you can’t kick her off.

It’s an old saying: “For the wide world old Miriam grieves, and at home without bread her children she leaves.” He’s sorry for the girl, but not sorry for his own son! Sling her round your neck and carry her about with you! That’s enough of such empty cackle!
There, don’t interrupt, let me have my say.
Eh! One only wears out one’s tongue with you.

The lass is hardworking and spruce, and keeps everything round herself﻿ ﻿… what d’you call it. And in our poverty, you know, it’s a pair of hands, I mean; and the wedding needn’t cost much. But the chief thing’s the offence, the offence to the lass, and she’s a what d’you call it, an orphan, you know; that’s what she is, and there’s the offence.
Eh! they’ll all tell you a tale of that sort﻿ ﻿…
Daddy Akím, you’d better listen to us women; we can tell you a thing or two.
And God, how about God? Isn’t she a human being, the lass? A what d’you call it﻿—also a human being I mean, before God. And how do you look at it?

That’s right, dear friend; you’ve cleared the way clean, as with water. Yes, let the lad speak for himself. Nowadays, you know, they’ll not let you force a son to marry; one must first of all ask the lad. He’ll never consent to marry her and disgrace himself, not for all the world. To my thinking, it’s best he should go on living with you and serving you as his master. And we need not take him home for the summer either; we can hire a help. If you would only give us ten roubles now, we’ll let him stay on.
All in good time. First let us settle one thing before we start another.

You see, Peter Ignátitch, I speak. ’Cos why? you know how it happens. We try to fix things up as seems best for ourselves, you know; and as to God, we what d’you call it, we forget Him. We think it’s best so, turn it our own way, and lo! we’ve got into a fix, you know. We think it will be best, I mean; and lo! it turns out much worse﻿—without God, I mean.
Of course one must not forget God.

It turns out worse! But when it’s the right way﻿—God’s way﻿—it what d’you call it, it gives one joy; seems pleasant, I mean. So I reckon, you see, get him, the lad, I mean, get him to marry her, to keep him from sin, I mean, and let him what d’you call it at home, as it’s lawful, I mean, while I go and get the job in town. The work is of the right sort﻿—it’s payin’, I mean. And in God’s sight it’s what d’you call it﻿—it’s best, I mean. Ain’t she an orphan? Here, for example, a year ago some fellows went and took timber from the steward﻿—thought they’d do the steward, you know. Yes, they did the steward, but they couldn’t what d’you call it﻿—do God, I mean. Well, and so﻿ ﻿…
Sits down and takes out his tobacco-pouch.
It seems there’s a complaint, you know, about you, Nikíta﻿—a complaint, I mean, a complaint.
Complaining? It’s a maid, an orphan maid, complaining, I mean. It’s her, you know﻿—a complaint against you, from Marína, I mean.
It’s I am asking you, and you must now, what d’you call it, give me an answer. Have you got mixed up with the lass, I mean﻿—mixed up, you know?
I don’t know what you mean. What’s up?
Foolin’, I mean, what d’you call it? foolin’. Have you been foolin’ with her, I mean?
Never mind what’s been! Of course one does have some fun with a cook now and then to while away the time. One plays the concertina and gets her to dance. What of that?
Don’t shuffle, Nikíta, but answer your father straight out.
Ah, Nikíta, mind! A lie will out. Did anything happen?
Well, Daddy Akím, how’s it to be?
Looks at his son, clicking his tongue disapprovingly.
Well, Daddy Akím, what do you say?
Why, the lad’s his own master, if only he what d’you call it.﻿ ﻿… I only wish that, what d’you call it, I mean.
You don’t know yourself what you’re jawing about. The lad himself has no wish to leave. Besides, what do we want with him at home? We can manage without him.
Only one thing, Daddy Akím﻿—if you are thinking of taking him back in summer, I don’t want him here for the winter. If he is to stay at all, it must be for the whole year.
And it’s for a year he’ll bind himself. If we want help when the press of work comes, we can hire help, and the lad shall remain with you. Only give us ten roubles now.﻿ ﻿…
Well then, is it to be for another year?
Well, if that’s settled we might step across to the inn and have a drink. Come, Daddy Akím, what do you say to a glass of vódka?
No, I never drink that sort of thing.
Ah, tea! yes, I do sin that way. Yes, tea’s the thing.
And the women will also have some tea. Come. And you, Nikíta, go and drive the sheep in and clear away the straw.
Enters with a rope, which she puts down. She takes off her outdoor things and goes into closet.
What, to look at you? I can see you well enough without.
Nikíta, there’s a person wants you. There is!
Marína from the railway; she’s out there, round the corner.

She wants you to come out. She says, “I only want to say a word to Nikíta.” I began asking, but she won’t tell, but only says, “Is it true he’s leaving you?” And I say, “No, only his father wanted to take him away and get him to marry, but he won’t, and is going to stay with us another year.” And she says, “For goodness’ sake send him out to me. I must see him,” she says, “I must say a word to him somehow.” She’s been waiting a long time. Why don’t you go?
Bother her! What should I go for?
She says, “If he don’t come, I’ll go into the hut to him.” Blest if she didn’t say she’d come in!
Not likely. She’ll wait a bit and then go away.
“Or is it,” she says, “that they want him to marry Akoulína?”
A likely thing! Who says it?
Who, you? Perhaps I might have afore, but I won’t now.
Who? My stepmother. She does nothing but grumble, and is always staring at you.
Well, you are strange! What have you come for?
That’s my name. What do you want with Nikíta? Well, what next? Go away, I tell you!
I see, you do want to throw me over.

Well, and what’s there to remember? You yourself don’t know. When you stood out there round the corner and sent Nan for me, and I didn’t come, wasn’t it plain enough that you’re not wanted? It seems pretty simple. So there﻿—go!
Not wanted! So now I’m not wanted! I believed you when you said you would love me. And now that you’ve ruined me, I’m not wanted.
Where’s the good of talking? This is quite improper. You’ve been telling tales to father. Now, do go away, will you?
You know yourself I never loved anyone but you. Whether you married me or not, I’d not have been angry. I’ve done you no wrong, then why have you left off caring for me? Why?
Where’s the use of baying at the moon? You go away. Goodness me! what a duffer!

It’s not that you deceived me when you promised to marry me that hurts, but that you’ve left off loving. No, it’s not that you’ve stopped loving me either, but that you’ve changed me for another, that’s what hurts. I know who it is!
What, will you strike me, then? Well then, strike me! What are you turning away for? Ah, Nikíta!
Supposing someone came in. Of course, it’s quite improper. And what’s the good of talking?
Takes his head in her hands and tries to kiss him.
Here’s a fine muddle. I’m as sweet as honey on the lasses, but when a fellow’s sinned with ’em it’s a bad lookout!

The scene represents the village street. To the left the outside of Peter’s hut, built of logs, with a porch in the middle; to the right of the hut the gates and a corner of the yard buildings. Anísya is beating hemp in the street near the corner of the yard. Six months have elapsed since the First Act.
He’s calling. You go and see what he wants, kicking up such a row.
Where? Why, he’s told me to go for Aunt Martha. “Fetch my sister,” he says. “I am going to die,” he says. “I have a word to say to her.”
Don’t go I tell you, I’ll go myself. You go and take the clothes to the river to rinse. Else you’ll not have finished by the evening.
But he told me to go.
You go and do as you’re bid. I tell you I’ll fetch Martha myself. Take the shirts off the fence.
The shirts? But maybe you’ll not go. He’s given the order.
Didn’t I say I’d go? Where’s Nan?
May the Lord help you, honey.
Looks round, stops working, and claps her hands with joy.
Ah, I’m driven well-nigh crazy. It’s awful!
Oh, don’t talk about it. He doesn’t live and doesn’t die!
But the money﻿—has he given it to anybody?
He’s just sending for his sister Martha﻿—probably about the money.
Well, naturally! But hasn’t he given it to anyone else?
To no one. I watch like a hawk.

He doesn’t let out. And I can’t find out in any way. He hides it now here, now there, and I can’t do anything because of Akoulína. Idiot though she is, she keeps watch, and is always about. Oh my poor head! I’m bothered to death.

Oh, my jewel, if he gives the money to anyone but you, you’ll never cease regretting it as long as you live! They’ll turn you out of house and home without anything. You’ve been worriting, and worriting all your life with one you don’t love, and will have to go a-begging when you are a widow.

No need to tell me, mother. My heart’s that weary, and I don’t know what to do. No one to get a bit of advice from. I told Nikíta, but he’s frightened of the job. The only thing he did was to tell me yesterday it was hidden under the floor.
Well, and did you look there?
I couldn’t. The old man himself was in the room. I notice that sometimes he carries it about on him, and sometimes he hides it.
About to answer, but sees neighbour and stops.
The neighbour (a woman) passes the hut, and listens to a call from within.
That’s the way he always coughs﻿—just as if he were screaming. He’s getting very bad.
Straight from home, dear. Come to see my son. Brought him some shirts﻿—can’t help thinking of these things, you see, when it’s one’s own child.
Well, and has he had communion?
Oh dear yes, the priest was here yesterday.
He came to, and creeps about again.
Well, and is he to have extreme unction?
The neighbours advise it. If he lives till tomorrow we’ll send for the priest.
Oh, Anísya dear, I should think your heart must be heavy. As the saying goes, “Not he is sick that’s ill in bed, but he that sits and waits in dread.”
Yes, if it were only over one way or other!
Yes, that’s true, dying for a year, it’s no joke. You’re bound hand and foot like that.

Ah, but a widow’s lot is also bitter. It’s all right as long as one’s young, but who’ll care for you when you’re old? Oh yes, old age is not pleasure. Just look at me. I’ve not walked very far, and yet am so footsore I don’t know how to stand. Where’s my son?
Ploughing. But you come in and we’ll get the samovar ready; the tea’ll set you up again.
Yes, you had better. And we’ve had a wedding down in our parts.
Ah, now if it were a poor man, then, as the saying is, it’s always unseasonable for a poor man to marry. But it’s Simon Matvéyitch, he’s married that Marína.
He’s a widower. I suppose there are children?
Four of ’em. What decent girl would have him! Well, so he’s taken her, and she’s glad. You see, the vessel was not sound, so the wine trickled out.
Oh my! And what do people say to it? And he, a rich peasant!
They are living well enough so far.
Yes, it’s true enough. Who wants to marry where there are children? There now, there’s our Michael. He’s such a fellow, dear me﻿ ﻿…
Hullo, Mávra. Where the devil are you? Go and drive the cow in.
Don’t speak about it. He’d better die of himself. It’s no use﻿—he doesn’t die, and I have only taken a sin on my soul. O-oh, my head, my head! Oh, why did you give me those powders?
What of the powders? The sleeping powders, lass﻿—why not give them? No evil can come of them.
I am not talking of the sleeping ones, but the others, the white ones.
Well, honey, those powders are medicinal.
Well, and did you use many?

I had a taste of the tea myself﻿—just a little bitter. And he drank them with the tea and says, “Even tea disgusts me,” and I say, “Everything tastes bitter when one’s sick.” But I felt that scared, mother.
Don’t go thinking about it. The more one thinks the worse it is.
I wish you’d never given them to me and led me into sin. When I think of it something seems to tear my heart. Oh dear, why did you give them to me?

What do you mean, honey? Lord help you! Why are you turning it on to me? Mind, lass, don’t go twisting matters from the sick on to the healthy. If anything were to happen, I stand aside! I know nothing! I’m aware of nothing! I’ll kiss the cross on it; I never gave you any kind of powders, never saw any, never heard of any, and never knew there were such powders. You think about yourself, lass. Why, we were talking about you the other day. “Poor thing, what torture she endures. The stepdaughter an idiot; the old man rotten, sucking her lifeblood. What wouldn’t one be ready to do in such a case!”
I’m not going to deny it. A life such as mine could make one do worse than that. It could make you hang yourself or throttle him. Is this a life?
That’s just it. There’s no time to stand gaping; the money must be found one way or other, and then he must have his tea.
O-oh, my head, my head! I can’t think what to do. I am so frightened; he’d better die of himself. I don’t want to have it on my soul.
I don’t know anything. He’s worried me to death.
What is it you don’t know? The business is clear. If you make a slip now, you’ll repent it all your life. He’ll give the money to his sister and you’ll be left without.
O-oh dear! Yes, and he did send for her﻿—I must go.
You wait a bit and light the samovar first. We’ll give him some tea and search him together﻿—we’ll find it, no fear.
Oh dear, oh dear; supposing something were to happen.
What now? What’s the good of waiting? Do you want the money to slip from your hand when it’s just in sight? You go and do as I say.
Well, I’ll go and light the samovar.
Holding on to the wall, creeps out into the porch and calls with a faint voice.
Has the girl gone for Martha? It’s very hard.﻿ ﻿… Oh, if only death would come quicker!
She had no time. I sent her to the river. Wait a bit, I’ll go myself when I’m ready.
Send Nan. Where’s she? Oh, I’m that bad! Oh, death’s at hand!
Oh dear! Then where is she?
Where’s she got to, the plague seize her!
Oh, dear! I can’t bear it. All my inside’s on fire. It’s as if a gimlet were boring me. Why have you left me as if I were a dog?﻿ ﻿… no one to give me a drink.﻿ ﻿… Oh﻿ ﻿… send Nan to me.
Here she is. Nan, go to father.
Go you. Oh﻿ ﻿… to Aunt Martha, tell her father wants her; say she’s to come, I want her.
Wait a bit. Tell her she’s to come quick. Tell her I’m dying. O-oh!

Ah yes, Peter Ignátitch, now I look at you I see, as the saying has it, “Sickness lives where men live.” You’ve shrivelled, shrivelled, all to nothing, poor dear, now I come to look at you. Seems illness does not add to good looks.

Oh well, Peter Ignátitch, it’s God’s will you know, you’ve had communion, and you’ll have unction, God willing. Your missus is a wise woman, the Lord be thanked; she’ll give you a good burial, and have prayers said for your soul, all most respectable! And my son, he’ll look after things meanwhile.
Why, if it’s money, or something, you can leave orders.
Let me sit here a bit for the last time. The air’s so stuffy inside. Oh, how bad I feel! Oh, my heart’s burning.﻿ ﻿… Oh, if death would only come.

If God don’t take a soul, the soul can’t go out. Death and life are in God’s will, Peter Ignátitch. You can’t be sure of death either. Maybe you’ll recover yet. There was a man in our village just like that, at the very point of death﻿ ﻿…
Leans back and shuts his eyes.
But have you searched everywhere? Under the floor?
No, it’s not there either. In the shed perhaps; he was rummaging there yesterday.

Go, search, search for all you’re worth. Go all over everywhere, as if you licked with your tongue! But I see he’ll die this very day, his nails are turning blue and his face looks earthy. Is the samovar ready?
The Lord be thanked, we’re all alive and have a crust to bite.
Well, let him sit. What’s it to me?
Why have you come back so early?
Have you done the strip beyond the bridge?
It’s too far to go there.
Well then﻿—o-oh!﻿ ﻿… Get out the seed potatoes, and the women will go and sort them.
What’s there to forgive? I’m a sinner myself.
I am sorry for him﻿—that sorry. How he cried! Oh dear!

Look at him﻿—seized with pity! He has found someone to pity too! He’s been treating you like a dog, and even just now was giving orders to have you turned out of the house. You’d better show me some pity!
What are you to be pitied for?
If he dies, and the money’s been hidden away﻿ ﻿…
No fear, he’ll not hide it﻿ ﻿…

Oh, Nikíta darling! he’s sent for his sister, and wants to give it to her. It will be a bad lookout for us. How are we going to live, if he gives her the money? They’ll turn me out of the house! You try and manage somehow! You said he went to the shed last night.
I saw him coming from there, but where he’s shoved it to, who can tell?
If you don’t keep wide awake now, then you may whistle for it. If his sister comes﻿—then goodbye to it!
That’s true. She’ll come and he’ll give it her. What’s to be done? Oh my poor head!
Don’t be talking now, but look alive, and I’ll keep his sister off if need be. Mind, don’t make a blunder! Get hold of the money and bring it here, and Nikíta will hide it.
Oh my head, my head! I don’t know how I’m going to﻿ ﻿…
Don’t talk about it I tell you, do as I bid you. Nikíta!
You stay here﻿—sit down﻿—in case something is wanted.
She was down in her daughter’s vegetable plot﻿—she’s coming.
There’s plenty of time if you do as I tell you.
I don’t know what to do; I know nothing, my brain’s all in a whirl. Nan! Go, daughter, and see to the calves, they’ll have run away, I’m afraid.﻿ ﻿… Oh dear, I haven’t the courage.
Go on! I should think the samovar’s boiling over.
Why, this affair﻿—how you’re to live your life.
How to live my life? Others live, and I shall live!
The old man will probably die today.
Well, if he dies, God give him rest! What’s that to me?
Keeps looking towards the porch while she speaks.
And what’s it you’ve been bothering about?

About your affairs, about your future. If you don’t take trouble in good time you’ll get nothing. You know Iván Moséitch? Well, I’ve been to him too. I went there the other day. I had something else to settle, you know. Well, so I sat and chatted awhile and then came to the point. “Tell me, Iván Moséitch,” says I, “how’s one to manage an affair of this kind? Supposing,” says I, “a peasant as is a widower married a second wife, and supposing all the children he has is a daughter by the first wife, and a daughter by the second. Then,” says I, “when that peasant dies, could an outsider get hold of the homestead by marrying the widow? Could he,” says I, “give both the daughters in marriage and remain master of the house himself?” “Yes, he could,” says he, “but,” says he, “it would mean a deal of trouble; still the thing could be managed by means of money, but if there’s no money it’s no good trying.”
unwraps her kerchief and takes out a paper
This paper’s only a decision for the elders to sign. There’s no great wisdom needed for that.

But you just hear what Iván Moséitch bids us do. “Above all,” he says, “mind and don’t let the money slip away, dame. If she don’t get hold of the money,” he says, “they’ll not let her do it. Money’s the great thing!” So look out, sonnie, things are coming to a head.
What’s that to me? The money’s hers﻿—so let her look out.

Ah, sonnie, how you look at it! How can a woman manage such affairs? Even if she does get the money, is she capable of arranging it all? One knows what a woman is! You’re a man anyhow. You can hide it, and all that. You see, you’ve after all got more sense, in case of anything happening.
Oh, your woman’s notions are all so inexpedient!
Why inexpedient? You just collar the money, and the woman’s in your hands. And then should she ever turn snappish you’d be able to tighten the reins!
Shows that she has something under her apron.
Give it to Nikíta, he’ll hide it. Nikíta, take it and hide it somewhere.
Well, give it here. I’ll shove it away somewhere.
Where will you shove it to?
Yes, he seems dead. He did not move when I took it.
Well there, I’ve done the sin and he has the money.﻿ ﻿…
Have done and go in! There’s Martha coming!

I’m from Zoúevo. I’m Nikíta’s mother from Zoúevo, my dearie. Good afternoon to you. He’s withering, withering away, poor dear﻿—your brother, I mean. He came out himself. “Send for my sister,” he said, “because,” said he﻿ ﻿… Dear me, why, I do believe, he’s dead!
Runs out screaming. Clings to a post, and begins wailing.
Send for the old women to lay out the body.
The same hut. Winter. Nine months have passed since Act II. Anísya, plainly dressed, sits before a loom weaving. Nan is on the oven.
An old labourer, enters, and slowly takes off his outdoor things.
Nikíta isn’t back from town, is he?
Must have been on the spree. Oh Lord!
Have you finished in the stackyard?
Picks at the corns on his hands.
What need has he to hurry? He’s got money. Merrymaking with that girl, I daresay﻿ ﻿…
Why shouldn’t one make merry if one has the money? And why did Akoulína go to town?
You’d better ask her. How do I know what the devil took her there!
What! to town? There’s all sorts of things to be got in town if one’s got the means. Oh Lord!

Mother, I heard myself. “I’ll get you a little shawl,” he says, blest if he didn’t; “you shall choose it yourself,” he says. And she got herself up so fine; she put on her velveteen coat and the French shawl.
Really, a girl’s modesty reaches only to the door. Step over the threshold and it’s forgotten. She is a shameless creature.
It’s time he was. Hasn’t he perhaps stopped at our inn? My sister, Thekla, says there’s heaps of sledges standing there as have come from the town.
You run to the inn and see! Mayhap, being drunk, he’s gone there.
Jumps down from the oven and dresses.
And he’s taken Akoulína with him?

Else he’d not have had any need of going. It’s because of her he’s unearthed all the business there. “Must go to the bank,” he says; “it’s time to receive the payments,” he says. But it’s all her fooling.
You only see if he’s there.
Oh dear, oh dear, what a fright he did give me! I had quite forgotten. But tell me, dear, I’ve heard someone’s been wooing Akoulína?
Gets up from the loom and sits down by the table.
They made some steps too, but it didn’t come off either. They won’t even see us.
Yet it’s time she was married.

Time and more than time! Ah, my dear, I’m that impatient to get her out of the house; but the matter does not come off. He does not wish it, nor she either. He’s not yet had enough of his beauty, you see.
Eh, eh, eh, what doings! Only think of it. Why, he’s her stepfather!

Ah, friend, they’ve taken me in completely. They’ve done me so fine it’s beyond saying. I, fool that I was, noticed nothing, suspected nothing, and so I married him. I guessed nothing, but they already understood one another.
So it went on from bad to worse, and I see they begin hiding from me. Ah, friend, I was that sick﻿—that sick of my life! It’s not as if I didn’t love him.
Ah, how hard it is to bear such treatment from him! Oh, how it hurts!
Yes, and I’ve heard say he’s becoming too free with his fists?

And that too! There was a time when he was gentle when he’d had a drop. He used to hit out before, but of me he was always fond! But now when he’s in a temper he goes for me and is ready to trample me under his feet. The other day he got both hands entangled in my hair so that I could hardly get away. And the girl’s worse than a serpent; it’s a wonder the earth bears such furies.
Ah, ah, my dear, now I look at you, you are a sufferer! To suffer like that is no joke. To have given shelter to a beggar, and he to lead you such a dance! Why don’t you pull in the reins?

Ah, but my dear, if it weren’t for my heart! Him as is gone was stern enough, still I could twist him about any way I liked; but with this one I can do nothing. As soon as I see him all my anger goes. I haven’t a grain of courage before him; I go about like a drowned hen.
Ah, neighbour, you must be under a spell. I’ve heard that Matryóna goes in for that sort of thing. It must be her.
Yes, dear; I think so myself sometimes. Gracious me, how hurt I feel at times! I’d like to tear him to pieces. But when I set eyes on him, my heart won’t go against him.
It’s plain you’re bewitched. It don’t take long to blight a body. There now, when I look at you, what you have dwindled to!

Growing a regular spindle-shanks. And just look at that fool Akoulína. Wasn’t the girl a regular untidy slattern, and just look at her now! Where has it all come from? Yes, he has fitted her out. She’s grown so smart, so puffed up, just like a bubble that’s ready to burst. And, though she’s a fool, she’s got it into her head, “I’m the mistress,” she says; “the house is mine; it’s me father wanted him to marry.” And she’s that vicious! Lord help us, when she gets into a rage she’s ready to tear the thatch off the house.
Oh dear, what a life yours is, now I come to look at you. And yet there’s people envying you: “They’re rich,” they say; but it seems that gold don’t keep tears from falling.
Much reason for envy indeed! And the riches, too, will soon be made ducks and drakes of. Dear me, how he squanders money!
But how’s it, dear, you’ve been so simple to give up the money? It’s yours.
Ah, if you knew all! The thing is that I’ve made one little mistake.
Well, if I were you, I’d go straight and have the law of him. The money’s yours; how dare he squander it? There’s no such rights.
They don’t pay heed to that nowadays.
Ah, my dear, now I come to look at you, you’ve got that weak.
Yes, quite weak, dear, quite weak. He’s got me into a regular fix. I don’t myself know anything. Oh, my poor head!
Crosses himself, knocks the snow off his feet, and takes off his coat.
How d’you do, father? Do you come straight from home?

I’ve been a-thinking, I’ll go and see what’s name, go to see my son, I mean﻿—my son. I didn’t start early﻿—had my dinner, I mean; I went, and it’s so what d’you call it﻿—so snowy, hard walking, and so there I’m what d’you call it﻿—late, I mean. And my son﻿—is he at home? At home? My son, I mean.
No; he’s gone to the town.
Ah, Mítritch! What are you, what d’ye call it, I mean?﻿ ﻿…
Why, I’m working for your son, Nikíta.
Dear me! What d’ye call﻿ ﻿… working for my son, I mean. Dear me!
But how’s that, what d’you call it, or what’s name, Nikíta, what does he do? Has he some business, I mean besides, that he should hire a labourer, a labourer I mean, hire a labourer?
What business should he have? He used to manage, but now he’s other things on his mind, so he’s hired a labourer.
Why shouldn’t he, seeing he has money?
Now that’s what d’you call it, that’s wrong, I mean, quite wrong, I mean. That’s spoiling oneself.
Oh, he has got spoilt, that spoilt, it’s just awful.
There now, what d’you call it, one thinks how to make things better, and it gets worse I mean. Riches spoil a man, spoil, I mean.

Fatness makes even a dog go mad; how’s one not to get spoilt by fat living? Myself now; how I went on with fat living. I drank for three weeks without being sober. I drank my last breeches. When I had nothing left, I gave it up. Now I’ve determined not to. Bother it!
And where’s what d’you call, your old woman?

My old woman has found her right place, old fellow. She’s hanging about the gin-shops in town. She’s a swell too; one eye knocked out, and the other black, and her muzzle twisted to one side. And she’s never sober; drat her!
Laying the table and serving up.
No, we don’t touch it. Only some twenty or thirty roubles as have come due; they must be taken.
Must be taken. Why take it, the money I mean? You’ll take some today I mean, and some tomorrow; and so you’ll what d’you call it, take it all, I mean.
We get this besides. The money is all safe.

All safe? How’s that, safe? You take it, and it what d’you call it, it’s all safe. How’s that? You put a heap of meal into a bin, or a barn, I mean, and go on taking meal, will it remain there what d’you call it, all safe I mean? That’s, what d’you call it, it’s cheating. You’d better find out, or else they’ll cheat you. Safe indeed! I mean you what d’ye call﻿ ﻿… you take it and it remains all safe there?
I know nothing about it. Iván Moséitch advised us at the time. “Put the money in the bank,” he said, “the money will be safe, and you’ll get interest,” he said.
That’s queer talk. How’s that﻿—what d’ye call, coming in, how’s that coming in, and they, who do they get it from I mean, the money I mean?
They take the money out of the bank.

Get along! ’Tain’t a thing a woman can understand! You look here, I’ll make it all clear to you. Mind and remember. You see, suppose you’ve got some money, and I, for instance, have spring coming on, my land’s idle, I’ve got no seeds, or I have to pay taxes. So, you see, I go to you. “Akím,” I say, “give us a ten-rouble note, and when I’ve harvested in autumn I’ll return it, and till two acres for you besides, for having obliged me!” And you, seeing I’ve something to fall back on﻿—a horse say, or a cow﻿—you say, “No, give two or three roubles for the obligation,” and there’s an end of it. I’m stuck in the mud, and can’t do without. So I say, “All right!” and take a tenner. In the autumn, when I’ve made my turnover, I bring it back, and you squeeze the extra three roubles out of me.
Yes, but that’s what peasants do when they what d’ye call it, when they forget God. It’s not honest, I mean, it’s no good, I mean.

You wait. You’ll see it comes just to the same thing. Now don’t forget how you’ve skinned me. And Anísya, say, has got some money lying idle. She does not know what to do with it, besides, she’s a woman, and does not know how to use it. She comes to you. “Couldn’t you make some profit with my money too?” she says. “Why not?” say you, and you wait. Before the summer I come again and say, “Give me another tenner, and I’ll be obliged.” Then you find out if my hide isn’t all gone, and if I can be skinned again you give me Anísya’s money. But supposing I’m clean shorn﻿—have nothing to eat﻿—then you see I can’t be fleeced any more, and you say, “Go your way, friend,” and you look out for another, and lend him your own and Anísya’s money and skin him. That’s what the bank is. So it goes round and round. It’s a cute thing, old fellow!

That, old fellow, is just what they’re fond of! And remember, them that are stupid, or the women folk, as can’t put their money into use themselves, they take it to the bank, and they there, deuce take ’em, clutch hold of it, and with this money they fleece the people. It’s a cute thing!
Not right? Eh, old fellow, who cares about that nowadays? And how clean they pluck you, too! That’s the fact of the matter.
Here’s a good girl, always busy! You’re cold, I should think?
Yes, I am, terribly. How d’you do, grandfather?
No. But Andriyán is there. He’s been to town, and he says he saw them at an inn in town. He says Dad’s as drunk as drunk can be!
Do you want anything to eat? Here you are.

Yes, she’s living all right. The little woman is what d’ye call it, clever and steady; she’s living, and what d’ye call it, doing her best. She’s all right; the little woman’s of the right sort I mean; painstaking and what d’ye call it, submissive; the little woman’s all right I mean, all right, you know.
And is there no talk in your village that a relative of Marína’s husband thinks of marrying our Akoulína? Have you heard nothing of it?

Ah; that’s Mirónof. Yes, the women did chatter something. But I didn’t pay heed, you know. It don’t interest me I mean, I don’t know anything. Yes, the old women did say something, but I’ve a bad memory, bad memory, I mean. But the Mirónofs are what d’ye call it, they’re all right, I mean they’re all right.
I’m that impatient to get her settled.
Goes on washing the spoons without turning her head.
Goes up and takes him by the arm.
Where have you learnt manners? The full name.
Laughs and pulls him by the arm.
That’s enough! You’re letting the cold in!
Say with which foot he steps? You’ve got to say it﻿—that’s flat.
You look who’s in the hut!
Bows and puts out his hand.
Drink, what’s that? I’ve been drinking? I’m to blame, that’s flat! I’ve had a glass with a friend, drank his health.
Go and lie down, I say.
Wife, say where am I standing?
Now then, it’s all right, lie down!
No, I’ll first drink a samovar with my parent. Go and light the samovar. Akoulína, I say, come here!
Why have you thrown everything about? Where’s the yarn?
The yarn? The yarn’s there. Hullo, Mítritch, where are you? Asleep? Asleep? Go and put the horse up.
Climbs down from the oven, and puts on felt boots.
Shall I really light the samovar?
The parcels? I’ve brought mine, the rest’s in the sledge. Hi, take this, this isn’t mine!
Goes on fidgeting with the leg-bands.
What d’you mean by that? “And it’s ill talking with one who is drunk”? But don’t you worry, let’s have some tea. And I can do anything; that’s flat! I can put everything to rights.
Puts his hand in his pocket, pulls out pocketbook, handles the notes in it and takes out a ten-rouble note.
I can’t, what d’you call it, I mean, can’t take it! And can’t what d’ye call it, talk to you, because you’re not yourself, I mean.
Takes it, and shakes his head.
The presents, what’s the use of showing ’em? I’ve put ’em away.
Get them, I tell you. Nan will like to see ’em. Undo the shawl. Give it here.
Gets out the parcels and puts them on the table.
Oh how lovely! It’s as good as Stepanída’s.
Brightening up and undoing the parcels.
Sweeps the shawl on to the floor with her arm.
Shows her a parcel and sits down on it.
Enough of your humbug. I’m not afraid of you. Whose money are you spreeing on and buying your fat wench presents with? Mine!
Pushes her while trying to pass.
What are you shoving for? I’ll teach you to shove!
Comes shoving herself in! You ought to keep quiet and remember your doings! You think no one knows!
Knows what? Out with it, out with it! What do they know?
You’re a slut who goes with another’s husband!
And you did yours to death!
Want to frighten me! I’m not afraid of you!
Where am I to go? I’ll not go out of my own house!
Be off, I tell you, and don’t dare to come in here!
I’ll go to the Elder! To the policeman!
I’ve turned her out, what more do you want?
She’s dirtied my new shawl. If that bitch hadn’t gone away, I’d have torn her eyes out!
That’s enough. Why should you be angry? Now if I loved her﻿ ﻿…

Loved her? She’s worth loving, with her fat mug! If you’d have given her up, then nothing would have happened. You should have sent her to the devil. And the house was mine all the same, and the money was mine! Says she is the mistress, but what sort of mistress is she to her husband? She’s a murderess, that’s what she is! She’ll serve you the same way!
Oh dear, how’s one to stop a woman’s jaw? You don’t yourself know what you’re jabbering about!
Yes, I do. I’ll not live with her! I’ll turn her out of the house! She can’t live here with me. The mistress indeed! She’s not the mistress﻿—that jailbird!

That’s enough! What have you to do with her? Don’t mind her. You look at me! I am the master! I do as I like. I’ve ceased to love her, and now I love you. I love who I like! The power is mine, she’s under me. That’s where I keep her. Points to his feet. A pity we’ve no concertina. Sings.

“We have loaves on the stoves, We have porridge on the shelf. So we’ll live and be gay, Making merry every day, And when death comes, Then we’ll die! We have loaves on the stoves, We have porridge on the shelf﻿ ﻿…”
Seems the women have been fighting again! Tearing each other’s hair. Oh Lord, gracious Nicholas!
Sitting on the edge of the oven, takes his leg-bands and shoes and begins putting them on.
Seems they can’t settle matters between them. Oh Lord!
Get out the liquor, we’ll have some with our tea.
She’s standing and crying out there in the passage.
Oh, that’s it! Call her, and tell her to bring the samovar. And you, Akoulína, get the tea things.
Unpacks spirits, rusks, and salt herrings.
Gets down and puts on his sheepskin, then comes up to the table and puts down the money.
Takes up his cap and belt.
My gracious! Where are you going to at this time of night?
I can’t, I mean what d’ye call ’em, in your house, what d’ye call ’em, can’t stay I mean, stay, can’t stay, forgive me.
But are you going without having any tea?
Eh now! Have done talking! Sit down and drink your tea!
Why, father, you’ll shame us before the neighbours. What has offended you?
Nothing what d’ye call it, nothing has offended me, nothing at all! I mean only, I see, what d’you call it, I mean, I see my son, to ruin I mean, to ruin, I mean my son’s on the road to ruin, I mean.
Ruin, ruin; you’re in the midst of it! What did I tell you that time?
You said all sorts of things!
I told you, what d’ye call it, I told you about the orphan lass. That you had wronged an orphan﻿—Marína, I mean, wronged her!
Eh! he’s at it again. Let bygones be bygones﻿ ﻿… All that’s past!
Sit down and drink your tea, and have done with it!
I can’t, I mean can’t what d’ye call it, can’t drink tea. Because of your filth, I mean; I feel what d’ye call it, I feel sick, very sick! I can’t what d’ye call it, I can’t drink tea with you.
Eh! There he goes rambling! Come to the table.
You’re in your riches same as in a net﻿—you’re in a net, I mean. Ah, Nikíta, it’s the soul that God needs!
Now really, what right have you to reprove me in my own house? Why do you keep on at me? Am I a child that you can pull by the hair? Nowadays those things have been dropped!
That’s true. I have heard that nowadays, what d’ye call it, that nowadays children pull their fathers’ beards, I mean! But that’s ruin, that’s ruin, I mean!
The money? There’s your money! I’ll go begging, begging I mean, before I’ll take it, I mean.
Takes a cup. All are silent.
The concertina? He’s bethought himself of it. Why, you took it to be mended. I’ve poured out your tea. Drink it!

Autumn. Evening. The moon is shining. The stage represents the interior of courtyard. The scenery at the back shows, in the middle, the back porch of the hut. To the right the winter half of the hut and the gate; to the left the summer half and the cellar. To the right of the stage is a shed. The sound of tipsy voices and shouts are heard from the hut.5 Second Neighbour Woman comes out of the hut and beckons to First Neighbour Woman.
How’s it Akoulína has not shown herself?

Why hasn’t she shown herself? She’d have been glad to; but she’s too ill, you know. The suitor’s relatives have come, and want to see the girl; and she, my dear, she’s lying in the cold hut and can’t come out, poor thing!
They say she’s been bewitched by an evil eye! She’s got pains in the stomach!
Dear me! There’s a go! But his relatives will surely find it out?

They find it out! They’re all drunk! Besides, they are chiefly after her dowry. Just think what they give with the girl! Two furs, my dear, six dresses, a French shawl, and I don’t know how many pieces of linen, and money as well﻿—two hundred roubles, it’s said!
That’s all very well, but even money can’t give much pleasure in the face of such a disgrace.
Hush!﻿ ﻿… There’s his father, I think.
They cease talking, and go into the hut.
The Suitor’s Father comes out of the hut hiccuping.

And I was just thinking, where’s the father? Where’s the father? And here you are, dear friend.﻿ ﻿… Well, dear friend, the Lord be thanked! Everything is as honourable as can be! When one’s arranging a match one should not boast. And I have never learnt to boast. But as you’ve come about the right business, so with the Lord’s help, you’ll be grateful to me all your life! She’s a wonderful girl! There’s no other like her in all the district!
That’s true enough, but how about the money?
Don’t you trouble about the money! All she had from her father goes with her. And it’s more than one gets easily, as things are nowadays. Three times fifty roubles!
We don’t complain, but it’s for our own child. Naturally we want to get the best we can.

I’ll tell you straight, friend: if it hadn’t been for me, you’d never have found anything like her! They’ve had an offer from the Karmílins, but I stood out against it. And as for the money, I’ll tell you truly: when her father, God be merciful to his soul, was dying, he gave orders that the widow should take Nikíta into the homestead﻿—of course I know all about it from my son﻿—and the money was to go to Akoulína. Why, another one might have thought of his own interests, but Nikíta gives everything clean! It’s no trifle. Fancy what a sum it is!
People are saying, that more money was left her? The lad’s sharp too!
Oh, dear soul alive! A slice in another’s hand always looks big; all she had will be handed over. I tell you, throw doubts to the wind and make all sure! What a girl she is! as fresh as a daisy!
That’s so. But my old woman and I were only wondering about the girl; why has she not come out? We’ve been thinking, suppose she’s sickly?

Oh, ah.﻿ ﻿… Who? She? Sickly? Why, there’s none to compare with her in the district. The girl’s as sound as a bell; you can’t pinch her. But you saw her the other day! And as for work, she’s wonderful! She’s a bit deaf, that’s true, but there are spots on the sun, you know. And her not coming out, you see, it’s from an evil eye! A spell’s been cast on her! And I know the bitch who’s done the business! They know of the betrothal and they bewitched her. But I know a counter-spell. The girl will get up tomorrow. Don’t you worry about the girl!
Well, of course, the thing’s settled.
Yes, of course! Don’t you turn back. And don’t forget me, I’ve had a lot of trouble. Don’t forget﻿ ﻿…
A woman’s voice from the hut.
If we are to go, let’s go. Come along, Iván!
Exeunt. Guests crowd together in the passage and prepare to go away.
Mother, come here, or they’ll hear.
Well? What is it? Where’s Akoulína?
She’s gone into the barn. It’s awful what’s she’s doing there! I’m blest! “I can’t bear it,” she says. “I’ll scream,” she says, “I’ll scream out loud.” Blest if she didn’t.
She’ll have to wait. We’ll see our visitors off first.

Oh mother! She’s so bad! And she’s angry too. “What’s the good of their drinking my health?” she says. “I shan’t marry,” she says. “I shall die,” she says. Mother, supposing she does die! It’s awful. I’m so frightened!
Comes in at the gate and begins collecting the scattered hay.
The guests are heard driving off.
Mítritch, you get off to sleep and I’ll put this straight.
All right, you throw it to the sheep. Well, have you seen ’em all off?
Yes, they’re off! But things are not right! I don’t know what to do!
But mind, Mítritch, don’t go blabbing.
What are you doing there? There’s no time to be lost! We must take it out directly!
I’ll tell you what you are to do. And you’ll have to do it!
You’d better take it to the Foundlings’﻿—if anything.
Then you’d better take it there yourself if you like! You’ve a hankering for smut, but you’re weak when it comes to settling up, I see!
Go down into the cellar, I tell you, and dig a hole!
Couldn’t you manage, somehow, some other way?
Mother! Grandmother’s calling! I think sister’s got a baby! I’m blest if it didn’t scream!
What are you babbling about? Plague take you! It’s kittens whining there. Go into the hut and sleep, or I’ll give it you!
Raising her arm as if to strike.
Why are you sitting there like a hen on a perch? What did your wife tell you to do? You just get things ready!
What do you mean to do?
We know what to do. You do your share!
You’ll be getting me into a mess!
What? You’re not thinking of backing out, are you? Now it’s come to this, and you back out!
Think what a thing it would be! It’s a living soul.

A living soul indeed! Why, it’s more dead than alive. And what’s one to do with it? Go and take it to the Foundlings’﻿—it will die just the same, and the rumour will get about, and people will talk, and the girl be left on our hands.

Not manage to do it in one’s own house? We’ll manage it so that no one will have an inkling. Only do as I tell you. We women can’t do it without a man. There, take the spade, and get it done there﻿—I’ll hold the light.
What am I to get done?
You’ll get me into a mess, bother you! I’ll go away! You do it alone as best you can!
Why have you come away? What have you done with it?
I’ve covered it with rags. No one can hear it. Well, has he dug it?
That’s enough now. Nikíta dear, why are you obstinate? What’s to be done now? One must take some trouble. Go, honey.

See the fine gentleman! He doesn’t like it! You’ve put upon me long enough! You’ve trampled me under foot! Now it’s my turn! Go, I tell you, or else I’ll do what I said.﻿ ﻿… There, take the spade; there, now go!
Yes, that’s just it, honey. If you know how to amuse yourself, you must know how to hide the consequences.
You stay with him, or he’ll go away, the wretch! And I’ll go and bring it.
Mind, don’t forget to baptize it, or I will if you like. Have you a cross?
See at end of Act, Variation, which may be used instead of the following.
Snatches the baby from him and throws it into the cellar.
Sits on the doorstep of the hut.
Sits looking at her and discourses.
Oh, oh! One would be glad not to sin, but what’s one to do?
It’s still alive! I can’t! It’s alive!
That’s because he’s so frightened! Never mind, it will pass!
Does not heed her, but listens by the cellar door.
Mother, my own mother, I can’t do any more! Can’t do any more! My own mother, have some pity on me!
Oh dear, how frightened you are, my darling! Come, come, drink a drop to give you courage!
Steps aside and sits down on the sledge.

Come, my own, have a drink! It certainly does seem uncanny at nighttime. But wait a bit. When the day breaks, you know, and one day and another passes, you’ll forget even to think of it. Wait a bit; when the girl’s married we’ll even forget to think of it. But you go and have a drink; have a drink! I’ll go and put things straight in the cellar myself.
Finds the spade, and goes down into the cellar.
He’s so frightened! You’ve been too hard with him. Leave him alone, he’ll come to his senses. God help him! I’ll set to work myself. Put the lantern down here. I can see.
Rushes out of the hut towards the cellar.
How can it whimper? Why, you’ve flattened it into a pancake! The whole head is smashed to bits!

The interior of the hut as in Act I.
Nan lies on the bench, and is covered with a coat. Mítritch is sitting on the oven smoking.
Approaches the lamp to put it out.
Jumps up, and remains sitting up.
Daddy darling! Don’t put it right out; leave a little bit if only as big as a mouse’s eye, else it’s so frightening!
And you are going to lie on the oven?
Tucks her up again, then stands up to go.
It gave just one cry, and now there’s nothing to be heard.
Oh Lord! Gracious Nicholas! What is it you can’t hear?
There is none, that’s why you can’t hear it.
But I heard it! Blest if I didn’t hear it! Such a thin voice!
Heard indeed! Much you heard! Well, if you know﻿—why then it was just such a little girl as you that the bogey popped into his bag and made off with.
Climbs up on to the oven.
Daddy! are you going to sleep?
What else? Do you think I’m going to sing songs?
Daddy! Daddy, I say! They are digging! they’re digging﻿—don’t you hear? Blest if they’re not, they’re digging!
What are you dreaming about? Digging! Digging in the night! Who’s digging? The cow’s rubbing herself, that’s all. Digging indeed! Go to sleep I tell you, else I’ll just put out the light!
Daddy darling, don’t put it out! I won’t﻿ ﻿… truly, truly, I won’t. It’s so frightful!
Frightful? Don’t be afraid and then it won’t be frightful. Look at her, she’s afraid, and then says it’s frightful. How can it help being frightful if you are afraid? Eh, what a stupid little girl!

Why, like this! When he finds such a one as you, who won’t sleep, he comes with a sack and pops the girl into it, then in he gets himself, head and all, lifts her dress, and gives her a fine whipping!
He takes a birch-broom with him.
But he can’t see there﻿—inside the sack!
No, friend, him you can’t bite!
Daddy, there’s someone coming! Who is it? Oh gracious goodness! Who can it be?
Well, if someone’s coming, let them come! What’s the matter with you? I suppose it’s your mother!
What’s the lamp burning for? We are going to sleep in the summer-hut.
Why, you see I’ve only just got straight. I’ll put the light out all right.
Rummages in her box and grumbles.
Why, what is it you are looking for?
I’m looking for a cross. Suppose it were to die unbaptized! It would be a sin, you know!
Of course it would! Everything in due order.﻿ ﻿… Have you found it?
That’s right, else I’d have lent her mine. Oh Lord!
It will die﻿—the little baby will! At Aunt Irene’s the old woman also baptized the baby, and it died!
If it dies, they’ll bury it!
But maybe it wouldn’t have died, only old Granny Matryóna’s there! Didn’t I hear what granny was saying? I heard her! Blest if I didn’t!
What did you hear? Go to sleep, I tell you. Cover yourself up, head and all, and let’s have an end of it!
If it lived, I’d nurse it!
Daddy! Eh, daddy! That girl, you know, you were telling about﻿—they didn’t kill her?
That girl? Oh yes. That girl turned out all right!
How was it? You were saying you found her?
But where did you find her? Do tell!

Why, in their own house; that’s where! We came to a village, the soldiers began hunting about in the house, when suddenly there’s that same little girl lying on the floor, flat on her stomach. We were going to give her a knock on the head, but all at once I felt that sorry, that I took her up in my arms; but no, she wouldn’t let me! Made herself so heavy, quite a hundredweight, and caught hold where she could with her hands, so that one couldn’t get them off! Well, so I began stroking her head. It was so bristly﻿—just like a hedgehog! So I stroked and stroked, and she quieted down at last. I soaked a bit of rusk and gave it her. She understood that, and began nibbling. What were we to do with her? We took her; took her, and began feeding and feeding her, and she got so used to us that we took her with us on the march, and so she went about with us. Ah, she was a fine girl!
Who can tell! They used to say, not altogether. ’Cos why, those people weren’t our own.
Yes; there now, so it is﻿ ﻿…
Covers up her head and cries.
The other day a traveller stayed the night; he said that when an infant died its soul goes up straight to heaven. Is that true?
Who can tell. I suppose so. Well?
Then you’d be off the list!
Up to ten one’s an infant, and maybe one’s soul would go to God. Else one’s sure to go to the bad!

And how to the bad? How should the likes of you not go to the bad? Who teaches you? What do you see? What do you hear? Only vileness! I, though I’ve not been taught much, still know a thing or two. I’m not quite like a peasant woman. A peasant woman, what is she? Just mud! There are many millions of the likes of you in Russia, and all as blind as moles﻿—knowing nothing! All sorts of spells: how to stop the cattle-plague with a plough, and how to cure children by putting them under the perches in the henhouse! That’s what they know!

Yes﻿—there it is﻿—just so! So many millions of girls and women, and all like beasts in a forest! As she grows up, so she dies! Never sees anything; never hears anything. A peasant﻿—he may learn something at the pub, or maybe in prison, or in the army﻿—as I did. But a woman? Let alone about God, she doesn’t even know rightly what Friday it is! Friday! Friday! But ask her what’s Friday? She don’t know! They’re like blind puppies, creeping about and poking their noses into the dung-heap.﻿ ﻿… All they know are their silly songs. Ho, ho, ho, ho! But what they mean by ho-ho, they don’t know themselves!
But I, daddy, I do know half the Lord’s Prayer!

A lot you know! But what can one expect of you? Who teaches you? Only a tipsy peasant﻿—with the strap perhaps! That’s all the teaching you get! I don’t know who’ll have to answer for you. For a recruit, the drill-sergeant or the corporal has to answer; but for the likes of you there’s no one responsible! Just as the cattle that have no herdsman are the most mischievous, so with you women﻿—you are the stupidest class! The most foolish class is yours!
That’s what one has to do.﻿ ﻿… You just cover up your head and sleep! Oh Lord!
Cover up your head, I tell you!
What have they done with me? What have they done with me?
Fetches the spirits and sets the bottle before him.
Give it here! Perhaps the drink will help me!
Mind! They’re not asleep! Here you are, have a drop!
What does it all mean? Why did you plan it? You might have taken it somewhere!
My own mother! My turn seems to have come! How it began to whimper, and how the little bones crunched﻿ ﻿… krr﻿ ﻿… I’m not a man now!
Go away from me! What have you done with me?
Go away from me! I’ll kill you! It’s all one to me now! I’ll kill you!
Oh, oh, how frightened he’s got! You should go and have a sleep now!
I have nowhere to go; I’m lost!
Now go, sonnie. You’ll fall asleep now all right.
Daddy dear, darling, they’ve smothered it!
See how they’ve frightened the girl.﻿ ﻿… What vile creatures they are! May the frogs kick them! Well then, climb up.

In front of scene a stack-stand, to the left a thrashing ground, to the right a barn. The barn doors are open. Straw is strewn about in the doorway. The hut with yard and outbuildings is seen in the background, whence proceed sounds of singing and of a tambourine. Two Girls are walking past the barn towards the hut.
Looks where the straw lies and sees someone.
Why, I thought he didn’t drink.
It seems he didn’t, until it was going around.
Just see! He must have come to fetch some straw. Look! he’s got a rope in his hand, and he’s fallen asleep.
Mammie says she is marrying against her will. Her stepfather threatened her, or else she’d not have done it for the world! Why, you know what they’ve been saying about her?
Going to the wedding, my dears?
It’s nearly over! We’ve come just to have a look.
Would you call my old man for me? Simon, from Zoúevo; but surely you know him?
To be sure we do; he’s a relative of the bridegroom’s, I think?
Of course; he’s my old man’s nephew, the bridegroom is.
Why don’t you go yourself? Fancy not going to a wedding!

I have no mind for it, and no time either. It’s time for us to be going home. We didn’t mean to come to the wedding. We were taking oats to town. We only stopped to feed the horse, and they made my old man go in.
Where did you put up then? At Fyódoritch’s?
Yes. Well then, I’ll stay here and you go and call him, my dear﻿—my old man. Call him, my pet, and say “Your missis, Marína, says you must go now!” His mates are harnessing.
Well, all right﻿—if you won’t go in yourself.
I have come for my old man.
Why didn’t you come to the wedding? You might have had a look round, and a laugh at my expense!
What have I to laugh at? I’ve come for my husband.
So I must not remember the past? You won’t let me?
It’s no use recalling the past! What used to be is over now!
And can never come back, you mean?
And will never come back! But why have you gone away? You, the master﻿—and to go away from the feast!

This is how it is: when I eat, it’s there! When I drink, it’s there! When I sleep, it’s there! I’m so sick of it﻿—so sick! But it’s chiefly because I’m all alone that I’m so sick, little Marína. I have no one to share my trouble.
You can’t live your life without trouble, Nikíta. However, I’ve wept over mine and wept it away.
Puts his hand to his throat.
Why, I’m sick of my whole life! I am sick of myself! Ah, Marína, why did you not know how to keep me? You’ve ruined me, and yourself too! Is this life?
Stands by the barn crying, but restrains herself.
takes hold of the rope on the straw

You think I’m joking? You think I’m drunk? I’m not drunk! Today even drink takes no hold on me! I’m devoured by misery! Misery is eating me up completely, so that I care for nothing! Oh, little Marína, it’s only with you I ever lived! Do you remember how we used to while away the nights together at the railway?
Don’t you rub the sores, Nikíta! I’m bound legally now, and you too. My sin has been forgiven, don’t disturb﻿ ﻿…
What shall I do with my heart? Where am I to turn to?
What’s there to be done? You’ve got a wife. Don’t go looking at others, but keep to your own! You loved Anísya, then go on loving her!
Oh, that Anísya, she’s gall and wormwood to me, but she’s round my feet like rank weeds!
Whatever she is, still she’s your wife.﻿ ﻿… But what’s the use of talking; you’d better go to your visitors, and send my husband to me.
Oh dear, if you knew the whole business﻿ ﻿… but there’s no good talking!
Marína! Missis! My old woman! are you here?
There’s your husband calling you. Go!
There she is, near the barn.
What are you standing there for? Come to the feast! The hosts want you to come and do them honour! The wedding party is just going to start, and then we can go too.
Rises and sits down on the straw.
I’m not saying anything! Don’t bother!
Takes the rope and makes a noose, and tries it on his neck.
Oh dear, what have you done with me? I’m a lost man!
But what is the matter then? Come, my own; come, give them your blessing, as is proper and honourable, and then it’ll all be over! Why, the people are waiting!
Why, in the usual way! Don’t you know?
I know, I know! But who is it I am to bless? What have I done to her?
What have you done? Eh, now he’s going to remember it! Why, who knows anything about it? Not a soul! And the girl is going of her own accord.

Because she’s afraid, of course. But still she’s going. Besides, what’s to be done now? She should have thought sooner! Now she can’t refuse. And his kinsfolk can’t take offence either. They saw the girl twice, and get money with her too! It’s all safe and sound!
Yes, but what’s in the cellar?
I’d be only too glad to forget it; but I can’t! When I let my mind go, it’s just as if I heard.﻿ ﻿… Oh, what have you done with me?
Now, what are you humbugging for?
Puts his hand to his throat.

Still it has to be done! As it is, people are talking. “The master’s gone away and won’t come; he can’t make up his mind to give his blessing.” They’ll be putting two and two together. As soon as they see you’re frightened they’ll begin guessing. “The thief none suspect who walks bold and erect!” But you’ll be getting out of the frying-pan into the fire! Above all, lad, don’t show it; don’t lose courage, else they’ll find out all the more!
Oh dear! You have snared me into a trap!
That’ll do, I tell you; come along! Come in and give your blessing, as is right and honourable;﻿—and there’s an end of the matter!
Oh, how nice it is, mother! So nice, so respectable! And how the people are pleased.﻿ ﻿… But where is he?
Here, honey, he’s here; he’s laid down on the straw and there he lies! He won’t come!
Then you should have stayed with them! What have you come for?
True enough, I must go back! Else what does it look like! The hosts both go and leave the visitors! And the guests are all of the best!
Gets up and brushes the straw off himself.
Exit women. Sits down and takes his boots off.
Takes the rope and pulls it.
Rises to his feet and begins getting the straw together, but reels for a time, then falls.

Why fear such muck as they are? You look at ’em in the bathhouse! All made of one paste! One has a bigger belly, another a smaller; that’s all the difference there is! Fancy being afraid of ’em! Deuce take ’em!
Why fear such muck as they are? You look at ’em in the bathhouse!

Interior of hut, full of people, some sitting round tables and others standing. In the front corner Akoulína and the Bridegroom. On one of the tables an Icon and a loaf of rye-bread. Among the visitors are Marína, her husband, and a Police Officer, also a Hired Driver, the Matchmaker, and the Best Man. The women are singing. Anísya carries round the drink. The singing stops.
If we are to go, let’s go! The church ain’t so near.
All right; you wait a bit till the stepfather has given his blessing. But where is he?
He is coming﻿—coming at once, dear friends! Have another glass all of you; don’t refuse!
Why is he so long? We’ve been waiting such a time!
They’ve sung all their songs, waiting here!
Holds his father’s arm and pushes him in before him.
I don’t like﻿—I mean what d’ye call it﻿ ﻿…
Go, take the icon, and give them your blessing!
What are you calling everybody for? Where should she be? How queer he seems!
Nikíta darling, what’s the matter with you? Oh my head, my head!
I did say he was taking too much of that French wine! Come to your senses; what are you about?
They try to lift him; he takes no heed of them, but looks in front of him.
Christian Commune! I have sinned, and I wish to confess!
Bows to the ground to her and rises.
Again bows to the ground before her.
And what are you drivelling about? It’s not becoming! No one wants to know! Get up! It’s like your impudence!
Get up, I tell you! Don’t be so impudent! What are you thinking about﻿—to recall it? Enough humbug! It’s shameful! Oh my poor head! He’s quite crazy!
The man’s beside himself! Lead him away!
The folk come up and try to seize him.
Motions them back with his arms.
Akoulína, I poisoned him! Forgive me, in Christ’s name!
What are you about? You sit still!
Oh Lord, what sins, what sins!
Seize him, and send for the Elder! We must draw up an indictment and have witnesses to it! Get up and come here!
Mind, old man, and don’t interfere! I have to draw up an indictment!

Eh, what a fellow you are; wait, I say! Don’t talk, I mean, about, what d’ye call it, ’ditements! Here God’s work is being done.﻿ ﻿… A man is confessing, I mean! And you, what d’ye call it﻿ ﻿… ’ditements!
Let God’s work be done, I mean, and then you, I mean, you do your business!
Bows to the ground before her.
I poisoned the father, dog that I am, and I ruined the daughter! She was in my power, and I ruined her, and her baby!
He raves! I told him to!
Bind him! The marriage is evidently off!
Men come up with their belts.
Bows to the ground before his father.
We will have the examination at once.
Goes and stands by his side.
